$comment: Built-in training program templates. See docs/adr/0007 for the terminology and the
rotation-not-calendar decision.
A SPLIT is how the body's musculature is divided across sessions -- full body, upper/lower,
push-pull-legs. A PROGRAM is the split plus exercise selection and a set prescription, which
is what these are. Progression is not in here: that is ProgressionEngine's job, session to
session, and baking target loads into a template would freeze them.
ORDERED, NOT SCHEDULED. No day-of-week appears anywhere, deliberately. 'Next in the rotation'
survives a missed Monday; 'it's Wednesday, do legs' starts nagging the first time life
happens.
EXERCISE ORDER IS SETUP ORDER. A Total Gym is one station that becomes a different station in
seconds -- but only when the next movement is set up like the last one. So movements that
share a position and a grip sit together, the squat stand goes on once, and where two
neighbours work unrelated muscles the app marks them as a pair to alternate. Ordering the same
exercises badly is the difference between a 30-minute session and a 45-minute one, and these
were ordered by src/client/src/session-plan.ts rather than by hand.
THIRTY MINUTES. Every session here is estimated to fit inside half an hour at its goal's rest
periods, with the set counts as written. A test enforces it. That is a real constraint on the
templates, and it is why the strength sessions have three movements rather than five: three
minutes of rest is the point of strength work, and pretending otherwise would produce a
program that lies about how long it takes.
Set counts here are the CEILING, not the starting point. A trainee new to this starts at one
set per movement and the plan grows as they show they want more -- see programs.ts.
The weekly total per muscle is what actually matters (docs/adr/0010), and the app computes it
from the rotation rather than asking anyone to do the arithmetic.
Every exerciseId must exist in exercises.json; a test enforces it.
RUNNABLE ON A STOCK MACHINE. Templates only plan movements that need no accessory or need one
marked `common` in exercises.json -- the squat stand and the wing. A shipped template that
assumes a leg pull accessory is a plan the trainee cannot follow on the machine they own, and
they find out one exercise at a time. A test enforces this too.
EMPHASIS is what the template is BUILT out of, and it is matched against what the trainee is
training for -- see ProgramEmphasis. It is not a difficulty rating and it does not change reps
or rest, which are the goal's job (GoalParameters).
lengthened      grow muscle: lead with movements loaded in the stretch, where this machine's
constant cable tension does the most work
largest-muscles lose fat: lead with the biggest muscles, because training barely dents the
calorie side and its real job in a deficit is keeping and adding lean mass
heavy-compounds get stronger: fewer movements, more sets on each
circuit         endurance: whole-body work with short rests
gentle          rehab: even coverage, nothing that pulls hard into a stretch
These are starting points, not prescriptions. The trainee can edit any of them, and build
their own from scratch.

templates.name: Full Body
templates.description: Three sessions a week, everything each time. The most forgiving split there is: miss a day and you have still trained every muscle group that week.
templates.bestFor: Starting out, or training two to three times a week.

templates.name: Upper / Lower
templates.description: Alternates upper body and lower body. Four sessions gets every muscle twice a week, which is the easiest way to fit real volume in without any one session dragging.
templates.bestFor: Training three to four times a week.

templates.name: Push / Pull / Legs
templates.description: Splits training by movement direction: pressing, pulling, then legs. Each session is short and focused, and nothing you train today is sore for tomorrow's.
templates.bestFor: Training three to six times a week.

templates.name: Big Muscle Full Body
templates.description: Built around legs, back and chest, with arms and calves picking up what the big movements already give them. While you are losing weight, muscle is what you are protecting — and the most of it sits below your waist.
templates.bestFor: Losing fat, or training two to three times a week with limited time.

templates.name: Strength Upper / Lower
templates.description: Fewer movements, more sets on each, and the hard ones first while you are fresh. Rest longer than feels necessary — that is what makes the next set heavy rather than tiring.
templates.bestFor: Getting stronger, training three to four times a week.

templates.name: Conditioning Circuit
templates.description: Whole-body sessions with short rests, so your heart rate stays up between sets. The load stays moderate on purpose — the work here is the pace, not the weight.
templates.bestFor: Building endurance, training three to five times a week.

templates.name: Gentle Full Body
templates.description: Even, controlled work across the whole body, with nothing that pulls hard into a stretch. Two sessions you can repeat as often as you are cleared to.
templates.bestFor: Working back from an injury, or easing in after time off.
